passage.title: The Fisherman's Lesson
passage.text:
Mang Isko had fished the same bay for forty years. Every dawn he pushed his small boat into the water and came back by noon with a basket of fish. But this year the baskets were lighter. Some days he came home with almost nothing.

His granddaughter Tess, who was in Grade 9, asked why. "The big boats with the fine nets take everything," he said. "Even the small fish that have not laid eggs yet. So next year there are fewer fish, and the year after, fewer still."

Tess read about this in school. Her teacher called it overfishing. The class wrote letters to the town council asking for a rule to protect the young fish. Tess read hers aloud at the meeting, her voice shaking at first, then growing steady.

The council agreed to set a no-fishing season in the bay for three months each year. Mang Isko grumbled about the lost days. But two years later, his basket was heavy again. "Your letter did that," he told Tess. She shook her head. "The fish did that. We just gave them time."

words.meaning: complained in a low, unhappy voice
words.example: He grumbled about the long line.

words.meaning: a group of people who make decisions for a town
words.example: The council voted to build a new park.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "lighter" in "this year the baskets were lighter" (paragraph 1)?
choices: emptier
heavier
smaller
darker
items.why: A lighter basket has fewer fish; a heavier one has more. The passage uses the antonym itself at the end: "his basket was heavy again."

items.prompt: According to Mang Isko, why were there fewer fish each year?
choices: The water got too cold.
Big boats caught even the young fish before they laid eggs.
Tess wrote letters.
He fished too close to shore.
items.why: He explains that the big boats take even the small fish "that have not laid eggs yet," so fewer fish are born.

choices: Tess was in Grade 9.
Big boats have fine nets.
Mang Isko explained that big boats take even the young fish, so fewer fish are born each year.
Fishing with big boats should be a crime.
items.why: It gives the cause and the result in one sentence. The first two are small details, and the last is an opinion the text does not state.

items.prompt: Why did Tess's class write letters to the town council?
choices: The teacher wanted a grade for writing.
They wanted to meet Mang Isko.
They wanted bigger nets for the small boats.
They wanted a rule to protect the young fish.
items.why: "The class wrote letters to the town council asking for a rule to protect the young fish."

items.prompt: "Her voice shaking at first, then growing steady." What does this show about Tess?
choices: She was nervous but became more confident.
She was cold.
She was angry at the council.
She could not read well.
items.why: A shaking voice shows nerves; a steady voice shows she gained confidence as she spoke.

items.prompt: Which word means almost the same as "steady" in "then growing steady" (paragraph 3)?
choices: shaky
firm
loud
quiet
items.why: Swap it in: "then growing firm" keeps the meaning. "Shaky" is the opposite; the text contrasts shaking with steady.

items.prompt: What happened BECAUSE the council set a no-fishing season?
choices: Mang Isko sold his boat.
The big boats came more often.
The fish had time to grow, and two years later the baskets were heavy again.
Tess stopped going to school.
items.why: "Two years later, his basket was heavy again." Tess explains the cause: "We just gave them time."

items.prompt: Why did Mang Isko grumble about the no-fishing season?
choices: He would lose three months of fishing, and the money that came with it.
He hated the council.
He wanted to fish with the big boats.
He did not believe Tess.
items.why: He "grumbled about the lost days." A fisherman who cannot fish for three months earns nothing in that time.

items.prompt: Which word means almost the same as grumbled?
choices: Cheered
Complained
Whispered
Laughed
items.why: To grumble is to complain in a low, unhappy voice.

items.prompt: Why did Tess say "The fish did that. We just gave them time"?
choices: She did not want credit; the rest came from letting the fish grow.
She was tired of fishing.
She thought her letter was bad.
She wanted her grandfather to stop fishing.
items.why: She shook her head at the praise and pointed out that protecting the fish, not her letter alone, fixed the problem.

choices: Mang Isko fished for forty years and liked to push his boat at dawn.
Fish were disappearing because of overfishing, so Tess and her class asked the council for a rule. The council made a no-fishing season, and the fish came back.
Tess's teacher taught the class a new word.
Big boats have fine nets.
items.why: This covers the problem, what Tess did, and the result, without small details.

items.prompt: Which detail should be LEFT OUT of a summary of the whole passage?
choices: The fish were disappearing because of overfishing.
Tess's class asked the council for a rule.
Mang Isko had fished the bay for forty years.
The no-fishing season brought the fish back.
items.why: How long he had fished does not change the story. Remove it and the summary still works; remove any of the other three and it falls apart.
